To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) 1 GeV iron ions cause cell death in mouse kidney epithelial cells and in kidney tissues in situ, but cells exposed in situ are less likely to die than those exposed in vitro; and 2) 1 Gev iron ions are mutagenically active in mouse kidney epithelia in vitro or in tissues in situ, with no apparent sparing of mutant fraction in the in situ exposures.
1 GeV/nucl iron ions cause cell killing in mouse kidney epithelial cells and that they are also mutagenic to these cells.
1 GeV iron ions are mutagenically effective in mouse kidney epithelial cells and that the mutation burden is not reduced by a prolonged incubation period in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mutagenic potency of high-energy heavy ions in mouse kidney, a tissue that is similar in structure to human kidney.
the mutagenic effects on mouse kidney epithelial cells of high-energy heavy-ion irradiation in vitro and in situ.
understanding the mutagenic and cytotoxic effects of heavy ion radiation in kidney epithelium, a target tissue for human cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mutagenic effect of high-energy heavy ions on the kidney in situ is comparable to that of in vitro irradiation, and the mutagenic effects are dose dependent.
the in vitro and in situ exposures are comparable for the induction of mutations at the Aprt locus, and both are mutagenic.
iron ions induce mutations in mouse kidney epithelial cells in vitro and in situ, with no sparing of mutations with prolonged incubation in situ.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in vitro exposures to iron ions result in cell death and mutation induction, and in situ exposure results in cell death, but the degree of mutation is not attenuated.

The main takeaway from our work is that
in vitro exposures of cells to heavy ions are a useful surrogate to in situ exposures in the mouse kidney.
in vitro exposures to high-energy iron ions may be used as a proxy for the in situ exposures.
